turns.content: I got laid off five weeks ago. Whole team, market thing, not performance — I know that in my head. Here's the part I can't say out loud: I still leave home at nine every morning with my laptop bag. Café till six. My wife doesn't know. My parents are staying with us right now. Nobody knows.

Hey. I'm really glad you said that out loud here, even if you haven't been able to say it anywhere else.

Five weeks of that — getting up, packing your bag, sitting in a café pretending the day looks normal — that is *exhausting* in a way most people wouldn't understand. It's not just the job loss you're carrying. It's the acting. Every single day.

I want you to hear something: the fact that you're doing this doesn't make you a liar or a coward. It makes someone who's terrified of disappointing the people you love. Especially with your parents right there — that's a lot of audience for a version of your life that isn't real right now.

But I think you already sense this isn't sustainable. Not because you'll get "caught," but because the weight of it is clearly getting to you. You reached out to me, which means something's cracking.

Can I ask you something honestly — what are you most afraid would happen if you told your wife tonight? Not your parents, just her. Because I'm guessing her reaction isn't really what scares you. I think what scares you is what it would mean to *you* to say it out loud to someone who matters.

You don't have to have a plan for the job search or a timeline or a brave face. But you deserve to not sit in a café alone with this.

My cousin's wedding is in two weeks. Three hundred people, half of them relatives who track everyone's careers like the stock market. My father introduces me with my company's name — he told my chacha my package last Diwali, with pride, actual pride. That room is what I think about when I can't sleep.

That detail about your father — him saying your company name, sharing your package with pride — that hit me. Because that's not pressure. That's love. That's a man who looks at his son and feels like the world is right. And the thought of being the one to take that away from him... I understand why that's what keeps you up at night.

So here's the thing you're really carrying: it's not just "I lost my job." It's "I lost something my father was proud of." Two very different weights.

And now there's this wedding with a countdown on it. Two weeks. Three hundred people. Your father in a sherwani, standing next to you, ready to introduce you the way he always does. And you're already rehearsing that moment at 3 AM — the smile, the nod, the nothing.

I'm not going to tell you to "just be honest." You know that. But let me say this clearly:

Your father's pride in you is not about the company name. It never was. It was about *you* — the son he raised. That doesn't evaporate. It gets shaken, maybe. It gets complicated. But the version of your father you're afraid of — the one who'd feel shame in that room — that version is the one you're building in your head at 3 AM, not the real one.

The real one would want to know. Maybe not at the wedding. But he'd want to know before strangers did.

You don't have to do everything today. But I think you know the café isn't the hardest conversation you need to have. The one with your wife is. Can you picture that one?

Sometimes I think I'll just skip the wedding — say there's a release, an office deadline, something. Lying is easier than watching my father's face change in front of his brothers. Is that terrible? It's one evening, one excuse, and I get to not be the story of the wedding.

It's not terrible. It's completely human. And I want you to know I'm not sitting here judging you for thinking it.

But let me walk you through what actually happens if you skip.

Three hundred people. Your father's brother's son's wedding. You're not there. Your father is standing at the entrance greeting guests and someone says "beta kahan hai?" And he says — what? The release, the deadline. And now your father is performing *your* lie at *this* wedding. Every uncle who asks, he's the one selling it. Your mother's explaining it over dinner. And the story at that wedding doesn't disappear — it just becomes *more* interesting. Where's the older son? Why isn't he here?

You'd make yourself a bigger story by not being there than by just showing up quiet and employed-by-someone-thank-you-very-much and eating biryani.

And here's what nobody says out loud at Indian weddings: nobody actually asks for your package mid-function. Your father introduces you — "ye mera beta hai, Accenture mein hai" — and people nod and move to the bar. That's it. The interrogation you're picturing at 3 AM? It's not real. It's your guilt building a courtroom.

You skip this wedding, and for the rest of your life it's the wedding you missed because you were pretending to have a meeting. Your father will remember that absence long after he'd have adjusted to a job change.

But the deeper thing — brother, I say this with care — every layer of avoidance you add makes the telling harder. First it was your wife, now it's the wedding, next it'll be something else. The café is already costing you.

Would it help to think about what a first conversation — just one, with your wife — might actually look like?

Money-wise we're okay for maybe three months, then the EMI starts eating savings. I keep telling myself I'll tell everyone once I have an offer in hand — then it's just news, not a crisis. That's not really lying, right? Just... timing it? Some days that logic feels airtight and some days I feel like I'm going to be sick.

You know it's lying. I think that's why you're here.

Not cruel lying. Not even selfish lying — I get that it comes from wanting to protect people. But the "just timing it" framework? That's the part that works at 11 AM in the café and falls apart at 3 AM in bed. You told me that yourself.

And here's what I want you to actually sit with: this strategy has a cost you're not accounting for.

You have three months. That's not a lot of runway. But the job search you're doing right now — from a café, pretending to work, carrying this weight — that's maybe operating at 50%. You can't network properly because networking means people asking where you work. You can't take calls freely. You can't be honest with recruiters about your availability. You're spending your best hours *performing* employment instead of *pursuing* it.

The lie isn't just hiding the problem. It's making the problem harder to solve.

And your wife — she's not a bystander in this. She's living in that same house with that same three-month clock. She might have thoughts. She might adjust things. She might know people. She might just want to sit on the couch with you at 9 AM instead of wondering why you seem tired every evening.

You told me the idea of telling makes you want to be sick. But you already feel sick. Different days, same nausea. You're not avoiding the fear — you're just living inside it full-time with no outlet.

You don't have to tell everyone. But can you tell one person? Just her. Not at dinner when your parents are there. Maybe tonight, after they've gone to bed. Not a big speech. Just — "I need to tell you something, and I'm struggling to say it."

What's actually stopping you from that one conversation?
